title: AVSAB 2025 Board Statement reaffirming Humane Dog Training
author: American Veterinary Society of Animal Behavior
finding: The board explicitly reaffirmed its 2021 recommendation for reward-based teaching and rejected the use of aversive training methods.
limits: Professional guidance synthesizing evidence; this statement itself is not a controlled trial or a credentialing endorsement.
use: Check that the app’s overall training approach remains consistent with current veterinary behavior guidance.

title: Dog bowling: Teach your dog to ten pin bowl
author: Dogs Trust behavior team
finding: A nose target can be developed into a floor-ball nudge and then movement toward lightweight pins.
limits: Practical enrichment guidance, not evidence of an anxiety treatment. Ball size, noise, ingestion risk and supervision matter.
use: Ball pushing, bowling and goal-game adaptations.

title: How to teach your dog to read
author: Dogs Trust behavior team
type: Original professional trick guide; critically screened
finding: The illustrated box game pairs spoken labels and gestures with going to designated boxes.
limits: Success does not by itself demonstrate reading printed language. Location, gestures and spoken cues may control behavior.
use: Inspired a clearly labeled optional visual-cue experiment; no claim of literacy or language comprehension is made.

title: How to Teach Your Dog to Weave Through Your Legs
author: Stephanie Gibeault, MSc, CPDT / American Kennel Club
finding: Separate comfortable passes around each side can be joined into a stationary figure eight, then optional walking passes.
limits: A trick guide, not a clinical intervention or an exercise prescription. Tight turns and handler clearance need individual judgment.
use: Comfortable middle position and slow stationary weave; cone alternatives for dogs that do not fit comfortably.

title: Teach Your Dog to Bow
author: AKC staff; demonstration by Nancy Field, CPDT-KA
access: Written steps reviewed; video not analyzed
finding: Describes building a bow, fading the food prompt and adding a cue.
limits: Not evidence that holding a bow treats anxiety or improves health. The app favors capturing a natural comfortable stretch and avoids physical positioning.
use: Optional short bow with no forced stretching or prolonged hold.

title: Successful Toothbrushing Training for Happy Dental Care
author: VCA Animal Hospitals
type: Veterinary professional care and training guide
access: Public written guide and dental-care advice
finding: Builds comfortable participation and small mouth-care components before introducing gentle brushing.
limits: Dental pain or oral disease needs a veterinary examination. Toothbrush size, pet-safe paste and technique should be selected with the veterinary team.
use: Voluntary toothbrushing preparation; no restraint, forced jaw opening, human toothpaste or dosing instructions.

title: Investigating responses to object-labels in the domestic dog (Canis familiaris)
author: Hanna Kőszegi, Claudia Fugazza, Lilla Magyari, Ivaylo B. Iotchev, Ádám Miklósi, Attila Andics
access: Article overview, methods and indexed findings
finding: Examines responses to spoken object labels while attempting to distinguish name learning from other cues.
limits: Typical and exceptional word-learning dogs differ. Selection, prior experience and subtle human cues complicate interpretation; this does not promise that every dog can learn item names.
use: Optional two-object choice experiment with side swaps, neutral body language and permission to stop.

title: Rapid learning of object names in dogs
author: Fugazza and colleagues / Scientific Reports
finding: Unusually experienced dogs learned labels in a social context; choosing a novel object by exclusion did not establish equivalent word learning.
limits: Exceptional dogs and small samples cannot establish a training timetable or ability threshold for ordinary pet dogs.
use: Avoiding exaggerated claims about toy-name games, ‘reading’, fast mapping or dog intelligence.

title: What is Trigger Stacking? How to Handle an Overly Stressed Dog
author: American Kennel Club training contributors
finding: Multiple close-together stressful events may leave a dog less able to cope with the next challenge.
limits: A practical description, not a precise hormone clock or evidence for a universal number of recovery hours.
use: Reducing demands after a difficult day, using individual baseline observations rather than fixed decompression deadlines.

title: Dog training tips
author: RSPCA
finding: Rewards, short enjoyable sessions and gradual teaching support basic cue learning.
limits: General professional guidance; no guarantee for a particular dog or the original lesson sequences.
use: Reward-based foundations, walking cues and optional tricks.

title: Crate training your dog
author: PDSA
finding: Voluntary introductions and gradual positive steps help make a suitable crate familiar.
limits: A crate is not a treatment for separation distress. This app stops at tiny attended closures, not prolonged confinement.
use: The separate attended crate-door lesson; exits and comfort remain available.

title: Fear Free Handling
author: SPCA New Zealand
finding: Supports voluntary participation in routine care using cooperative approaches and low-stress handling.
limits: A professional position statement, not a validated protocol for each care task. Pain and actual procedures need individual veterinary guidance.
use: Start signals, stopping at withdrawal, and preparation rather than forced handling.

title: Scent Work: Get Started
author: American Kennel Club
finding: Recreational scent work joins finding a scent with communicating the find to a handler.
limits: The app uses secured familiar-human cotton samples without essential oils. Its games are original adaptations and do not establish competition readiness or operational detection.
use: Separate scent search, indication and cooperative report components.

title: Walking 1-2-3
author: CattleDog Publishing veterinary behavior education team
finding: Describes a predictable counting and reward pattern and credits Leslie McDevitt’s Control Unleashed pattern games.
limits: Practical teaching guidance, not a clinical trial or a guarantee that the game will make trigger exposure safe.
use: A short quiet count-and-walk adaptation with optional participation and no fear-exposure requirement.

title: Tracking: Get Started
author: American Kennel Club
finding: Distinguishes following a human-laid scent route from simply finding a visible person or article.
limits: A competition overview is not a validated training protocol. This app’s fresh tiny trails do not qualify a dog for sport or search-and-rescue work.
use: Separating a recreational human-route-following exercise from visual hide-and-seek and food trails.
